OIIX.name: FIR Tehran
OIIX.conflictType: Interstate conflict — Iran vs Israel/US (fragile ceasefire)
OIIX.narrative: EASA's CZIB-2026-04 reflects a ceasefire that has held since April 2026 but remains fragile, with an elevated Iranian air-defence posture that raises the risk of civil aircraft being misidentified. EASA has warned escalation could resume with little notice. The eastern OIIX/Tehran FIR was partially reopened for overflights in June 2026 while the western part remains closed; very few international operators are using the FIR, with most Europe-Asia traffic routing south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. The shoot-down of Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran in Jan 2020 illustrates how quickly the situation can deteriorate. Key events: March 2026 — FIR closed following large-scale US and Israeli strikes and subsequent Iranian missile/drone retaliation; June 2026 — eastern portion partially reopened; July 2026 — EASA CZIB continues to advise operators not to operate at any altitude.

cross.detail: Some overflights above FL285 are possible via specific temporary routes linking Oman/UAE with Central Asia, the Caucasus and Turkey, but western Iran remains heavily restricted. Several radar systems remain degraded, many western airports are still closed or daytime-only, and most operators continue avoiding the airspace.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Several states continue to warn against operations in Iranian airspace. EASA continues to advise operators not to operate in the OIIX/Tehran FIR at any altitude. Earlier events (June 2025: Israel-Iran missile exchange; Oct 2024: mutual missile attacks) are captured in the narrative.

ORBB.name: FIR Baghdad
ORBB.conflictType: Non-state armed groups (IBMGs) + Iranian missile/drone spillover
ORBB.narrative: Despite the regional ceasefire, EASA cites recurrent Iranian drone and ballistic-missile strikes reaching Iraqi airspace, alongside the continued presence of Iranian-backed militant groups (IBMGs), as reasons the Baghdad FIR remains a do-not-operate zone. The FIR reopened to overflights in June 2026 following the US-Iran ceasefire, with north-south routes available, but most Europe-Asia traffic still routes south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. Primary risks include missile and drone activity, misidentification by air-defence systems operated by local and foreign military forces, and terrorist groups possessing portable anti-aircraft weaponry. Key events: March 2026 — FIR closed following US/Israeli strikes on Iran and Iranian retaliation; June 2026 — reopened for overflights; July 2026 — EASA CZIB continues to advise operators not to operate at any altitude.

cross.detail: Iraq is open for overflights, but it does not restore the old Europe-Asia corridor because western Iran remains restricted and most operators still consider the ORBB/Baghdad FIR too high risk. Some airlines are using it; main flows remain north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan or south via Egypt/Saudi/Oman.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Iraqi airspace remains open to some operators, but EASA continues to advise against operations at any altitude. Earlier events (June 2025: airspace closed during Israel-Iran exchange; Apr 2024: Iran drone/missile strike on Israel; Apr 2023: drone/missile attacks in northern Iraq; Oct 2021: FAA permitted overflights above FL320) are captured in the narrative.

OLBB.name: FIR Beirut
OLBB.narrative: A Trilateral Framework Agreement between Israel, Lebanon and the US (26 June 2026) is a step toward consolidating the ceasefire, but EASA notes its long-term implementation is uncertain, and that Lebanon has not shown it can proactively manage airspace risk.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon continue, and most international operators continue to avoid the OLBB/Beirut FIR. Primary risks: military activity linked to the Israel-Hezbollah conflict, including missile and drone activity. Some states allow limited operations to OLBA/Beirut provided arrivals and departures remain over the Mediterranean Sea. GNSS spoofing and jamming have been reported in the FIR since Nov 2023. Key events: Feb–Jul 2026 — Israeli airstrikes continued despite repeated ceasefire extensions; Oct 2024 — Israel launched a ground operation against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon; July 2026 — EASA CZIB continues to advise operators not to operate at any altitude.

OJAC.name: FIR Amman
OJAC.conflictType: Missile/drone overflight risk (regional spillover, no direct conflict on Jordanian soil)
OJAC.narrative: Jordan's airspace has repeatedly seen Iranian missiles and drones pass through en route to other targets, intercepted by Jordanian and allied air defences. Jordanian authorities have not published any airspace restrictions of their own despite this activity. The FIR remains open and operating normally; EASA has issued an Information Note advising operators to factor the potential risk into their planning. Key events: Apr 2024 — Jordan temporarily closed airspace during the Iranian drone and missile attack on Israel; Oct 2023 — Jordan intercepted drones and missiles transiting its airspace; Feb–Jul 2026 — Jordan remained open throughout the Iran conflict; July 2026 — EASA issued a new Information Note following renewed military activity in the Gulf.

cross.detail: Open and operating normally. In practice, it is still not a major transit route for Europe-Asia traffic; most operators continue to route via Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. The OJAC/Amman FIR remains open and operating normally. Primary risk is missile and drone activity from regional conflicts crossing Jordanian airspace. Key events are captured in the narrative above.

OKAC.name: FIR Kuwait
OKAC.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OKAC.narrative: Kuwait hosts major US military facilities, making it a plausible target for Iranian retaliation and increasing the risk of civil aircraft being caught up in an attack or an air-defence response. The OKAC/Kuwait FIR is currently open for arrivals and departures only — overflights remain prohibited — with restrictions extended until at least 4 August 2026. OKKK/Kuwait airport and other military targets in Kuwait were struck by missiles and drones in March 2026. Key events: March 2026 — missile and drone strikes damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport; Feb–Jul 2026 — FIR closed and reopened several times; July 2026 — EASA CZIB advises operators not to operate at any altitude.

cross.detail: Kuwait has extended airspace restrictions until at least Aug 4. Overflights through the OKAC/Kuwait FIR are not permitted; only flights arriving to or departing from OKKK/Kuwait are allowed, with prior approval.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. The OKAC/Kuwait FIR remains open for arrivals and departures only; overflights continue to be prohibited. EASA advises operators not to operate at any altitude. Key events are captured in the narrative above.

OBBB.name: FIR Bahrain
OBBB.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OBBB.narrative: As with Kuwait and Qatar, the US military presence in Bahrain is the main driver of EASA's risk assessment for this FIR. Bahrain is open to overflights; the FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before returning to normal overflight operations. Iranian missile and drone attacks targeted several Gulf states in March 2026, with incidents affecting airspace around Bahrain. EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate at any altitude, and nearby restrictions — particularly Kuwait — can affect routing.

cross.detail: Bahrain is open to overflights. Note that nearby airspace, especially Kuwait, remains restricted and can affect routing.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. The OBBB/Bahrain FIR remains open to overflights, but EASA advises operators not to operate at any altitude. Bahrain lies close to several key military facilities in the Gulf region. Key events are captured in the narrative above.

OTDF.name: FIR Doha
OTDF.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OTDF.narrative: Qatar hosts significant US forces and has itself been targeted by Iranian strikes during the recent escalation, keeping it on EASA's do-not-operate list even as operational conditions ease. Qatar is open and operating largely normally following several closures and reopenings during the Iran conflict. A missile strike was reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha in March 2026. Some temporary restricted areas and residual military activity remain. EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate at any altitude.

cross.detail: Qatar has reopened to overflights. Earlier restrictions on waypoints and arrival/departure route segments have been withdrawn, though some temporary restricted areas and military activity remain.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. The OTDF/Doha FIR remains open and largely normal, but EASA advises operators not to operate at any altitude. Qatar was directly affected during the conflict, including missile strikes near Doha. Key events are captured in the narrative above.

OMAE.name: FIR Emirates
OMAE.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OMAE.narrative: The UAE's proximity to the Strait of Hormuz and its role as a regional hub keep it firmly within EASA's risk assessment, despite being operationally busy.

cross.detail: The UAE remains open to overflights, with traffic managed through normal ATS routes and temporary RNAV corridors. GPS interference continues to be a significant operational issue across the FIR. EASA advises operators to avoid the FIR at all levels.

OOMM.name: FIR Muscat — west of 58°E only
OOMM.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OOMM.narrative: Unlike other Gulf FIRs, only the western portion of Omani/Gulf of Oman waters is covered — reflecting where commercial vessel attacks and Strait of Hormuz tension actually concentrate. Oman remained open throughout the Iran conflict and became a key part of the main southern bypass route (Egypt-Saudi-Oman) carrying significant Europe-Asia overflight traffic. EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E. Flow measures and GNSS interference reports are ongoing.

cross.detail: Oman remains one of the most useful FIRs in the region for the southern bypass. It is open but still part of the managed corridor system, with flow measures and ongoing GNSS interference reports.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. The OOMM/Muscat FIR remains open and is a key part of the southern bypass route. Primary risk is spillover of missile or drone activity from conflicts elsewhere in the region. EASA's CZIB restriction (west of 58°E, Gulf of Oman waters) and key events are captured in the narrative above.

OSTT.name: FIR Damascus
OSTT.narrative: EASA's longest-running Middle East bulletin (19 revisions since 2017) reflects a still-unresolved multi-actor conflict. Traffic patterns have shifted: OSTT quietly reopened to some regional carriers in early 2025 as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq corridor, even though most Western operators continue to avoid it. Primary risks include military activity linked to the Syrian conflict, Israeli airstrikes targeting Iranian and Hezbollah-linked positions, and the potential for misidentification by air-defence systems. Key events: Sep 2018 — Russian IL-20 shot down in error near the Syria-Cyprus FIR boundary; Feb 2020 — A320 approaching Damascus diverted after being caught in crossfire during Israeli airstrikes; Oct 2023 — airstrikes damaged runways at OSDI/Damascus and OSAP/Aleppo; Dec 2024 — airspace temporarily closed following the fall of the Assad regime; Jan–Jul 2026 — gradual increase in overflights as some regional operators use OSTT as an alternative to Iran/Iraq; March 2026 — FIR closed following US/Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent retaliation.

cross.detail: Syria has quietly become part of the regional routing picture again after years of almost no international overflight traffic.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. Syrian airspace remains high risk; several countries continue to prohibit or advise against operations in the OSTT/Damascus FIR due to risk from military operations, anti-aviation weaponry and unstable security conditions. Some regional operators have started using it as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq routing. Key events are captured in the narrative above.

OYSC.name: FIR Sana'a only
OYSC.conflictType: Civil war + interstate spillover (Red Sea attacks)
OYSC.narrative: This bulletin covers only the Sana'a FIR, not the whole of Yemen. The ongoing civil war and Houthi involvement in the wider regional conflict keep the risk assessment unchanged since 2017.

cross.detail: Yemen remains an active conflict zone, and the vast majority of Yemeni airspace (OYSC/Sanaa FIR) should be avoided. Several countries prohibit aircraft from overflying any land portion of the FIR. US operators can still use offshore routes UT702 and M999, while other countries permit flights on overwater portions of Yemeni airspace. Saudi airspace to the north and Somali airspace to the south also have risks. The primary risk is intentional targeting by terrorist groups with access to sophisticated anti-aircraft weaponry. Civil aircraft may also be at risk from high-intensity military operations including explosive drones and missiles. Saudi and Israeli airstrikes can occur at any time, including in the capital Sana'a. Major events: Jul 2026: Yemen's government carried out an airstrike on the runway at OYSN/Sanaa Airport to stop an Iranian aircraft from landing. Dec 2024 - ongoing: OYSN/Sanaa Airport closed due to damage from Israeli airstrikes in Dec 2024 and May 2025. Jan 2024: US and UK carried out airstrikes against Houthi rebels in Yemen in response to missile and drone attacks in the Red Sea. Sep 2023: Houthi drone attacks near the Yemen-Saudi border. Apr-Oct 2022: All parties agreed a ceasefire. 2018-2022: Frequent Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa and other targets in retaliation for Houthi drone attacks. 2017: OYSN/Sanaa Airport badly damaged by coalition airstrikes.

UUWV.name: FIR Moscow and others (west of 60°E)
UUWV.conflictType: Interstate war — Russian invasion of Ukraine (air-defence risk)
UUWV.narrative: Issued after the likely accidental shoot-down of Azerbaijan Airlines flight 8243 near Grozny in December 2024, this bulletin reflects the risk that Russian air-defence systems responding to Ukrainian strikes pose to civil aircraft, compounded by widespread GNSS interference.

cross.detail: As of June 2025, drone attacks across Russia are increasing, with some reaching as far as Siberia, raising risk for any aircraft still using Russian airspace. Hundreds of drones have been shot down recently, including in areas around Moscow. Russian air-defence systems use surface-to-air missiles capable of reaching all altitudes, so the risk applies at every level. Most operators avoid Russian airspace completely; those still flying there should be prepared for sudden closures or reroutes. Most activity occurs at night, but daytime disruptions are now common. Ukraine's airspace has remained fully closed to civil aviation since the Russian invasion in Feb 2022. Several countries prohibit operators from using Russian airspace near FIR boundaries with Ukraine. The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military near the Russia-Ukraine border, including misidentification (as with MAS17, UIA752). Major events: Jan 2025: EASA issued a new CZIB recommending against flights in western Russia (west of 60°E) due to threat of anti-aircraft fire and high danger of misidentification by air-defence systems targeting Ukrainian drones and missiles — following the shoot-down of a passenger jet at URMG/Grozny on Dec 25. Jan 2024: Crash of a military transport aircraft near Belgorod, approx 20nm from the Ukrainian border; both Russia and Ukraine accused each other of shooting it down. Aug 2023: Private jet carrying Wagner mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin crashed en route from Moscow to St Petersburg on Aug 23; speculation centred on a bomb onboard. Jul 2023 - ongoing: Recurring drone strikes on targets in Moscow and surrounding region, with some drones damaging buildings and Moscow airports being forced to close temporarily on multiple occasions.

UKBV.name: All Ukrainian FIRs
UKBV.narrative: In force since the day of the invasion, this remains one of the clearest and most stable prohibitions in this dataset — Ukraine itself has closed its FIRs to civil traffic by NOTAM.

cross.detail: Ukraine closed its entire airspace to all civil traffic on Feb 24, 2022, due to a military invasion by Russia. There is ongoing active conflict between Russian and Ukrainian forces. Russia, Belarus and Moldova have closed large sections of their own airspace near FIR boundaries with Ukraine. All major countries that regularly issue airspace warnings (the US, UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy) have issued total flight bans for Ukraine. The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military, including misidentification (as with MAS17, UIA752). The secondary risk is potential loss of Ukrainian ATC service at short notice (e.g. cyber attack) and other unforeseeable non-normal operating environments. Prior to February 2022, there were two areas of concern: the conflict in the far east of the country (affecting UKDV/Dnipro FIR) and the double claim over ATC and airspace in Crimea (UKFV/URFV/Simferopol FIR).

HSSS.name: FIR Khartoum
HSSS.conflictType: Civil war — Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) vs Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
HSSS.narrative: The ongoing SAF–RSF civil war has put anti-aircraft artillery, MANPADS and SAM systems into play across the whole of Sudanese airspace, keeping the entire Khartoum FIR off-limits.

cross.detail: Following a military coup in April 2023, Sudan remains closed to all civilian flights. In South Sudan, air navigation services remain suspended above FL245. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed, but no NOTAMs are being issued. A Contingency Plan with published overflight routes via HSPN/Port Sudan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and South Sudan is available. Several countries have issued airspace warnings advising operators not to enter Sudanese airspace due to risks from anti-aircraft weaponry and military activity. The primary risk is security on the ground for any unplanned diversions; throughout the conflict, passenger jets have been targeted by gunfire at HSSK/Khartoum Airport. The secondary risk is Sudan's proximity to South Sudan, which has poor ATC provision for overflights below FL245. Major events: Nov 2025: Il-76 reportedly shot down by a surface-to-air missile near Babanusa, southern Sudan. May 2025: Drone attack targeting critical infrastructure including HSPN/Port Sudan airport. Oct 2024: Foreign-registered cargo aircraft shot down by local militia over North Darfur, near the border with Chad. Apr 2023: Military coup on Apr 15; Sudan's airspace closed, South Sudan's airspace closed above FL245. Oct 2021: Military coup on Oct 25; HSSK/Khartoum airport closed for two days with all flights suspended.

HLLL.name: FIR Tripoli
HLLL.narrative: Libya's two rival governments and various non-state armed actors create a real risk of misidentification when crossing between areas controlled by different authorities. The one carve-out is for coastal airport approaches made from over the sea.
HLLL.restrictionLabel: Do not operate, except flights to coastal airports approached from the sea, subject to ATC contact and your own risk assessment

cross.detail: A civil war has been ongoing since 2014. Libyan airspace (HLLL/Tripoli FIR) should be avoided entirely. The primary risk is misidentification by Libyan air-defence systems, or by militia who have threatened to shoot down aircraft operating in western Libya, including at HLLM/Tripoli Mitiga airport. Military activity has been reported over the high seas, operating as OAT or without ATC contact. Reliable ATC services cannot be guaranteed; there have been regular ATS and radar outages and severe VHF limitations across the FIR, with operators having to communicate with Malta ATC for guidance. Total flight ban for US operators; several other countries have warnings in place. Major events: Aug 2023: Major evacuation of aircraft from Tripoli due to violent clashes and gunfire at Mitiga airport. Jul 2023: Italy cancelled its 10-year ban on flights to/from Libya. Aug 2022: Militia air-defence forces claimed to have shot down a US drone near Benghazi. Jun 2022: Failed militia attempt to seize government offices in Tripoli; armed clashes led to suspension of flights at HLLM/Mitiga airport. Jan 2020: Multiple airstrikes targeting HLLM/Mitiga airport. Nov 2019: Militia advancing on Tripoli declared a no-fly-zone around the city, threatening to shoot down civil aircraft attempting to fly to HLLM/Mitiga airport. 2014: HLLT/Tripoli airport closed after clashes between rival militias destroyed most of its facilities; remains closed to this day.

DRRR.name: Malian territory, especially the north-east
DRRR.conflictType: Insurgency — non-state armed groups active across the Sahel
DRRR.narrative: Non-state armed groups operating in Mali, particularly in the north-east, are assessed to have MANPADS and SAM missile capability, which is why the restriction is altitude-based rather than a total ban.

cross.detail: The conflict in northern and central Mali has continued since 2012 and the security situation remains volatile. Several countries have airspace warnings in place, typically advising operations at or above FL250 or FL260 and avoiding GATB/Timbuktu, GAGO/Gao and GAKL/Kidal. The US advises caution at all levels due to ongoing fighting, expanding militant activity, and a state-run paramilitary force operating anti-aircraft systems, military aircraft, UAS and electronic warfare equipment. Primary risks include MANPADS and other surface-to-air weapons, indirect fire near airports, and potential misidentification or spillover from military activity. Low-level and airport-phase operations carry the highest exposure. ATS in Mali is provided by the GOOO/Dakar and DRRR/Niamey FIRs, with a long-standing restriction for overflights of Mali to published ATS routes at FL320 and above. Major events: April 2026: Security situation escalated sharply; on April 25 multiple armed groups carried out coordinated attacks nationwide against state and military targets, with gunfire and explosions reported near GABS/Bamako. France issued a new airspace warning advising French operators not to operate to/from GABS or use it as an alternate. Sep 2024: Insurgents breached GABS/Bamako and set the presidential jet on fire; multiple attacks occurred across the city and the airport closed temporarily. Dec 2023: Germany prohibited its operators below FL260 in northern Mali; commercial flights to GATB/Timbuktu cancelled after shelling near the airport; a military jet crashed near GAGO/Gao, possibly shot down. Aug 2020: All airports closed for two days during a military coup; Bamako ACC remained operational and overflights were unaffected. Apr 2018: Militants attacked UN bases near GATB/Timbuktu using indirect fire and vehicle bombs. Jan 2017 and Nov 2016: Vehicle bomb and rocket attacks targeted GAGO/Gao and GATB/Timbuktu airports.

HCSM.name: Somali airspace
HCSM.conflictType: Insurgency — Al-Shabaab and related terrorist groups
HCSM.narrative: Terrorist organisations operating in Somalia are assessed to have confirmed anti-aircraft weaponry, possibly including MANPADS, driving the same FL260 altitude floor as Mali.

cross.detail: The security situation in Somalia is highly unstable. The central government has little control of major cities and ports, with ongoing extremist militant attacks targeting civilians and aviation interests. The primary risk is to overflying aircraft at lower flight levels, which may be targeted by anti-aircraft-capable weapons. The US prohibits flights across the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR below FL260, except for flights transiting the overwater portion going to/from HDAM/Djibouti airport. Several other countries have issued warnings advising against operating below FL260. A secondary risk exists from unauthorised ATC units contacting aircraft and issuing climb/descent instructions that conflict with official ones from Mogadishu Control. From Nov 2025, Somaliland has said all overflights require a PPR from its own CAA, while Somalia has reaffirmed through an AIC that it controls the entire FIR — expect conflicting permit instructions near Hargeisa and northern Somalia. Major events: Feb 2024: Multiple reports of aircraft within the Mogadishu FIR being contacted by a fake controller issuing conflicting instructions. Aug 2023: Reports of uncontrolled operations including combat helicopters flying at low levels (FL030) without position or routing reports. Oct 2022: Somalian government warned that HCMM/Mogadishu airport may be targeted by militant groups. May 2022: Class A airspace implemented in the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR above FL245. 2020-ongoing: Multiple Al-Shabaab attacks on HCMM/Mogadishu and nearby targets. May 2020: An Embraer EMB-120 was shot down on approach to Bardale airstrip, killing all six people on board — an accidental shoot-down by Ethiopian forces.

OPKR.name: Baluchistan province (partial)
OPKR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPKR.narrative: Violent non-state actor (VNSA) groups with confirmed MANPADS operate in Baluchistan. The Kashmir dispute separately raises misidentification risk further north.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. In May 2025 there was a period of intense cross-border shelling and aerial activity in Kashmir; a ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held, but the situation remains fragile. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions; current guidance generally advises operators to remain at or above FL260. Primary risks are from anti-aviation weaponry including potential MANPADS below FL260, and inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures issued and commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in Kashmir; ceasefire announced May 10 has largely held; some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan, highlighting cross-border military activity risk. Dec 2023 - ongoing: GPS spoofing reports in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in Kashmir.

OPLR.name: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province (partial)
OPLR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPLR.narrative: Covers the north-western province, where the Kashmir dispute adds a misidentification risk on top of the VNSA activity common to both restricted Pakistani provinces.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. In May 2025 there was a period of intense cross-border shelling and aerial activity in Kashmir; a ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held, but the situation remains fragile. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions; current guidance generally advises operators to remain at or above FL260. Primary risks are from anti-aviation weaponry including potential MANPADS below FL260, and inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures issued and commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in Kashmir; ceasefire announced May 10 has largely held; some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan, highlighting cross-border military activity risk. Dec 2023 - ongoing: GPS spoofing reports in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in Kashmir.

OAKX.name: FIR Kabul
OAKX.conflictType: Post-conflict security vacuum — extremist groups active, limited air traffic services
OAKX.narrative: Since the 2021 Taliban takeover, Afghanistan has had little to no functioning air traffic control. The Kabul FIR is Class G airspace: crews use published contingency routes and TIBA procedures rather than normal ATC clearances. Some countries restrict overflights to airways P500 and G500 in the far east of the FIR; others allow overflights across the entire airspace at and above FL320. Traffic through the FIR increased in March 2026 as flights used the northern bypass around the closed Middle East corridor. Key events: Aug 2021 — US and allied forces withdrew; OAKX/Kabul FIR became uncontrolled Class G airspace; Feb 2026 — cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated, commercial traffic continued via P500 and G500; March 2026 — traffic further increased due to Middle East corridor closures.

cross.detail: The OAKX/Kabul FIR remains Class G with no normal ATS service; crews must use published contingency routes and TIBA procedures. Armenia and Azerbaijan remain important parts of the northern bypass, with steady overflight demand through the region.

March 2026: Afghanistan's airspace remains open but has no ATC service. Traffic has increased as flights use the northern bypass to avoid the closed central Middle East corridor. Primary risk is surface-to-air fire at low altitudes; additionally, there is no ATC service and an extreme threat to crew safety and security on the ground. Contingency route and FL320 floor details, and key events, are captured in the narrative above.

HAAA.name: FIR Addis Ababa, north of 8.5°N
HAAA.conflictType: Regional/border tension — assessed by EASA as medium risk
HAAA.narrative: This is an EASA Information Note, not a CZIB — meaning EASA's risk assessment group judged the risk here as medium rather than high. Full analytical detail is restricted to the CZ Hub.
HAAA.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: The airspace risk picture in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region (Ethiopia/Eritrea border) has been improving since a peace deal was agreed in early Nov 2022, but airspace warnings remain in place. The primary risk is from large-scale ceasefire violations involving missiles or anti-aircraft weaponry that could affect overflights — civil aircraft being mistaken for military interest or caught in crossfire. Major events: Feb 2024: New fighting flared up in the Amhara region (south of Tigray), including air strikes. Nov 2022: Peace deal agreed in the Tigray region; Ethiopian Airlines planned to resume flights to HAMK/Mekele airport. Nov 2021: Several western countries issued airspace and travel warnings for the Tigray region following increased fighting. Jul 2021: HAAA/Addis FIR NOTAM closed a section of airspace below FL290 over the Tigray following reports that militia shot down a military transport plane near Mekele. Nov 2020: Major escalation in the Tigray region; some airways closed by Ethiopian and Sudanese CAAs; multiple airports targeted by rockets and missiles, including HHAS/Asmara, HABD/Bahir Dar and HAGN/Gondar. Sep 2018: Hidden ATC strike by Ethiopian controllers; unqualified replacements provided, with significant limitations.

VYYF.name: FIR Yangon, below FL260
VYYF.conflictType: Internal armed conflict — assessed by EASA as medium risk
VYYF.narrative: As with Ethiopia, this is a medium-risk Information Note rather than a do-not-operate CZIB. France's own national guidance goes slightly further operationally, setting a hard altitude floor.
VYYF.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: The security situation in Myanmar has deteriorated since the military coup in Feb 2021, with conflict and violence across many parts of the country involving air strikes and armed clashes. Several countries have issued airspace warnings at lower flight levels due to the potential risk from military operations, surface-to-air fire and anti-aviation weaponry. GPS jamming (and possibly spoofing) has been reported in the north of the FIR for overflights between China and Bangladesh airspace. Major events: Jan 2024: Armed group shot down a military helicopter in the northern state of Kachin using what was likely a MANPAD. Sep 2023: Several attacks by rebel groups on military targets, including a makeshift drone dropping bombs on aircraft hangars at an airbase next to VYNT/Naypyitaw airport; also intermittent GPS jamming reports on airway N895. Apr 2023: VYYY/Yangon airport temporarily closed following attack with improvised artillery rounds. Sep 2022: A Myanmar National Airlines passenger was reportedly shot as bullets passed through the fuselage of an ATR 72 on approach to VYLK/Loikaw. Feb 2021: Military coup ousted the government; ATC strike at end of Feb resulted in no ATC service for overflights, followed by increasing strikes, mass protests and armed clashes.
